info:
In Russian, the predicate (what you say about the subject) can function as the verb by itself in the present tense.

English uses “to be” as a grammatical placeholder:
I am tired
She is a teacher
The verb often carries almost no meaning — it just holds tense and agreement.

Russian often drops the copula entirely in the present tense and lets the word endings, the case system, or a special particle, carry the grammatical load.

So instead of:
subject + verb + predicate
Russian often uses:
subject + predicate
And that predicate behaves like a verb in the sentence.

Why this works in Russian:
Russian grammar already encodes:
who the subject is (endings, pronouns)
whether something exists (нет)
location and state (cases, prepositions)
negation (не)
So an extra “is” is redundant.
English needs syntax to do this.
Russian uses morphology and particles.

info:
нужно — “need to / must / it is necessary”

It is an impersonal predicate, not a normal verb with a subject.
There is no grammatical subject: the sentence is built around necessity, not who acts.
The person is added indirectly (often with датив):
Мне нужно работать — “I need to work.”
Тебе нужно уйти — “You need to leave.”
How it differs from English:
English ties obligation to the subject (“I need”), while Russian treats necessity as a state of the situation, with the person only marked as the one affected.
